newsitem.title: GERMANY: Duisenberg voices doubts on stability council idea.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg voices doubts on stability council idea.

text.p: Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg poured cold water on French proposals to set up a stability council as a counterweight to the planned European Central Bank, saying the European Union did not need new institutions.
But he added that it would be normal and in line with the Maastricht Treaty for finance ministers to hold meetings.

This would be necessary, for example, if they intended to find an exchange rate arrangement for the euro against the dollar along the lines of the Plaza or Louvre currency accords, which was the domain of governments, he said.

"I don't know what the proposals mean," Duisenberg, who is tipped to head the ECB after the planned launch of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), told Die Welt newspaper in an interview published on Tuesday.

"According to my information, they refer to the setting up of informal meetings by finance ministers participating in the euro. That in itself is a perfectly normal thing. It is also possible under the Maastricht Treaty.

"But whether it is sensible to call this meeting a stability council is another matter. We don't need new institutions in the the Union. But the French have in the meantime, denied that these formal meetings should be a counterweight to the European Central Bank."

Asked whether he saw a danger that a stability council may lead to the EMU having two voices on monetary policy, Duisenberg said "This danger can arise. But exchange rate relations, for example against the dollar, are the domain of governments.
"If there were to be an exchange rate arrangement between the euro and the dollar zones, which I do not think probable in the short term, that would be a matter for the ministers.

"And the finance ministers would have to speak with one voice. That is why they would have to meet to discuss a joint position. The implementation of such an arrangement, comparable with the Louvre or Plaza Accord, would then be the responsibility of the ECB.
"But the ECB's main priority is to guarantee price stability."
Duisenberg also said the three Benelux countries, Germany, France, Austria, Finland and Ireland would probably be among the first states to form EMU at the scheduled starting date on January 1, 1999.

While other countries were making "impressive" efforts to meet the criteria it remained open whether they would make it in time. "But it's not a catastrophe if one, two, three, four countries join a little later," Duisenberg said.

Duisenberg, however, told another German newspaper, business daily Boersen Zeitung, that he expected all 15 European Union members to have joined the currency union by 2002, when the new coins will be issued.

It was not enough for countries to get their budget deficits in shape just for 1997, the key year for deciding which EU members can join, Duisenberg said. Medium-term budget prospects also had to be assessed.
Duisenberg is scheduled to become president of the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner to the European Central bank, this summer.
